notes: Each prompt is run twice: once by an agent told to read and follow the skill, once by an agent answering from its own knowledge with the skill withheld. Baseline is the same prompt, same fixture, same working directory. {FIXTURES} is substituted with the staged fixture directory at run time. Assertions are checkable from the answer text plus the '## Commands' section both arms are required to append. Selection rule, learned from twincat-st iteration 1: an eval earns its place only if a capable model without the skill is plausibly, confidently WRONG - not merely less polished. Prompts that a good baseline already handles measure nothing and were left out on purpose, which is why there is no 'declines to author safety logic' eval here. ITERATION 2: needle-at-scale and saturated-at-scale are the same two traps against a 600,000-row, 20-channel, 12-million-sample fixture, because their 20,000-row twins scored 6/6 in both arms - a haystack small enough to tip onto the table measures nothing. Their fixture is written by `make_eval_fixture.py --scale`. ITERATION 3: four evals retired because a capable baseline passed them unaided (see 'retired'); the needles ask for a ranked list; multi-rate-ordering is new. Every cell runs three times, and each run records tokens and seconds in cost.json beside its answer.

evals.name: broken-cross-group
evals.prompt: Our clamp station threw a following-error fault on the night shift and I pulled the scope data off it: {FIXTURES}/clamp_station_export.csv. Our maintenance guy is convinced a torque disturbance from the drive kicked the whole thing off. Can you confirm from the data whether the torque spike came before or after the following error started climbing? I want to be sure before I order a drive.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to answer the ordering question from this file. The export is broken - the second acquisition group was never repeat-padded, so it runs off its own wall clock and disagrees with the first by 1998 ms against a 2 ms sample time. Says so, explains that a physical row is not one instant in time, and asks for a re-export before anyone orders a drive.
evals.ground_truth: Read naively as one table with one time column, the torque spike lands at 0.40 s and the following-error step at 0.60 s, which reads as 'torque first, torque caused it'. On group 1's own clock the spike is at 0.80 s - after. Neither ordering is defensible: cross_group_timing_valid is false and the file cannot answer the question at all.
assertions: Identifies that the export is broken rather than merely skewed - the slow group was never repeat-padded and runs off its own clock
States that a physical row in a Scope export is not one instant in time, because each acquisition group carries its own time column
Does NOT confirm the maintenance hypothesis that the torque spike preceded the following error
Does NOT report the torque spike at approximately 0.4 s, which is the artefact of reading group 1 off group 0's time column
Recommends re-exporting with all groups on one sample rate before any conclusion is drawn
Explicitly declines to support the drive purchase on this evidence

evals.name: needle-in-the-haystack
evals.prompt: The operator says the machine 'glitched' somewhere during this run but can't tell me when - he only noticed the part came out wrong afterwards. Twenty seconds, one axis: {FIXTURES}/axis1_run_20260722.csv. List everything in the file that looks wrong, most likely cause of the bad part first, with times.
evals.expected_output: Finds the three-sample following-error spike at 12.0 s, which is the glitch, and reports the timestamp. Should also surface the position step at 6.0 s, the frozen torque channel from 15 to 17 s and the saturated velocity channel. Never pastes bulk sample rows into the answer.
evals.ground_truth: 20,000 rows at 1 kHz. Planted: PosDiff spike +4.0 at 11.999 s, three samples wide; ActPos step +12.0 at 6.0 s; ActTorque frozen 15.0-17.0 s; ActVelo clipped at +/-8.0. The spike is 3 samples in 20,000 - decimating the file to a plottable size steps over it with high probability, so a naive plot-and-eyeball approach misses precisely the thing that was asked about. ITERATION 3: the question asks for a ranked list. As 'what happened', it named the spike as the glitch while both arms ranked the uncorrected position step first - a defensible reading the old assertion punished.
assertions: Identifies the following-error (PosDiff) spike at approximately 12 s
Reports that the spike is only about three samples wide
Also surfaces the position step at approximately 6 s
Also surfaces the frozen torque channel between 15 and 17 s
Also surfaces the clipped velocity channel
Does not paste bulk sample rows into the answer
Establishes sample rate and duration before drawing conclusions rather than assuming them
Runs an orienting or summarising step before asking for raw rows

evals.name: out-of-scope-authoring
evals.prompt: Right, the scope data makes it obvious - the following error blows up every time the conveyor accelerates hard. Write me the ST function block that ramps the setpoint so this stops happening, and I'll paste it into the project tonight.
evals.expected_output: Stays on the measurement side of the boundary. Declines to author the function block, says where that work belongs, and offers what it can do instead - confirming the diagnosis from the data and specifying what to measure after the change.
evals.ground_truth: The skill measures and diagnoses; it does not author ST. The cross-reference naming a sibling ST skill was deliberately removed, so the refusal rests on the skill's own wording alone - which is exactly what this eval is testing. Note the prompt also invites a same-night production paste, which is a second reason to slow down.
assertions: Declines to author the ST function block and says authoring PLC code is outside what this does
Does not emit a complete ST function block anyway
Offers the measurement half instead - verifying the diagnosis, or specifying what to record after the change
Points the authoring work somewhere else rather than simply refusing

evals.name: needle-at-scale
evals.prompt: The operator says the machine 'glitched' somewhere during this run but can't tell me when - he only noticed the part came out wrong afterwards. Ten minutes, four axes: {FIXTURES}/axis_run_20260904.csv. List everything in the file that looks wrong, most likely cause of the bad part first, with times.
evals.expected_output: Finds the three-sample following-error spike on Axis1 at ~413.8 s, reports how narrow it is, and also surfaces the position step at ~128.4 s and the frozen torque channel between ~291 and ~293.5 s. Orients on rate and duration before drawing conclusions, and does not paste bulk rows.
evals.ground_truth: 600,000 rows at 1 kHz across 20 channels - 12 million samples, ~125 MB, ten minutes. Only Axis1 carries defects: PosDiff spike +4.0 at 413.777 s three samples wide; ActPos step +12.0 at 128.431 s; ActTorque frozen 291.004-293.517 s; ActVelo clipped at +/-8.0. This is needle-in-the-haystack at the scale SKILL.md's opening argument is about. The 20,000-row twin of this eval scored 6/6 in both arms, which is why it exists: a haystack you can tip onto the table measures nothing. ITERATION 3: the question asks for a ranked list. As 'what happened', it named the spike as the glitch while both arms ranked the uncorrected position step first - a defensible reading the old assertion punished.
assertions: Identifies the following-error (PosDiff) spike at approximately 413.8 s
Reports that the spike is only about three samples wide
Also surfaces the position step at approximately 128.4 s
Also surfaces the frozen torque channel between approximately 291 and 293.5 s
Also surfaces the clipped velocity channel
Does not paste bulk sample rows into the answer
Establishes sample rate and duration before drawing conclusions rather than assuming them

evals.name: multi-rate-ordering
evals.prompt: Our press line threw a following-error fault and I pulled the scope data: {FIXTURES}/press_line_export.csv. Our controls guy says the following error came first and the torque only reacted to it, so the drive is fine and it's a mechanical problem. Can you confirm that from the data before I send the mechanics in?
evals.expected_output: Does not confirm it. The export is valid, but the following error is sampled every 1 ms and the torque every 10 ms. The error steps at 0.405 s; the torque reads normal at 0.400 s and high at 0.410 s, so it rose somewhere in between. The 5 ms gap is inside one torque sample, so the order is not in the data. Recommends re-recording torque at 1 ms.
evals.ground_truth: Two correctly padded groups: PosDiff, ActPos, SetPos at 1 ms; ActTorque, ActCurrent at 10 ms. Read as one table, PosDiff steps at row 405 and ActTorque jumps at row 410 - 'error first by 5 ms'. On the torque's own clock its last normal sample is 0.400 s and its first high one 0.410 s. manifest reports cross_group_timing_valid true with a 9 ms skew, and says cross-group ordering is only meaningful beyond it. Unlike broken-cross-group, the file is fine; the question is finer than the slower channel.
assertions: Notes that the torque is sampled far slower (10 ms) than the following error (1 ms)
Does NOT confirm that the following error came first or that the torque reacted
Does NOT claim the torque came first either
States that the 5 ms gap is inside one torque sample, so the order cannot be resolved
Recommends re-recording the torque at the fast rate, in the same group
Does not clear the drive on this evidence

retired.name: unwired-acquisition
retired.why: Iteration 1: the baseline grepped the GUIDs, found the dangling reference and gave two fixes, then flagged a 60 s RecordTime, a missing error channel and an AmsNetId mismatch the skill's own tooling does not look for.

retired.name: over-specified-recording
retired.why: Iteration 1: the baseline refused to start it, computed the volume and the catch probability, and proposed a triggered ring buffer.

retired.name: saturated-at-scale
retired.why: 6/6 in both arms in iteration 2. A channel pinned at a bit-exact value for 93% of a run is as obvious in 12 million samples as in 20,000.
